body: WorldCom grew via ~60 acquisitions (MCI for ~$37 bn in 1998); stock peaked ~$64 in mid-1999 and the company filed for bankruptcy on 21 Jul 2002 (then the largest US bankruptcy, ~$107 bn assets). In Jun 2002 internal auditor Cynthia Cooper's team found >$3.8 bn of line costs (fees paid to other carriers) improperly capitalised as capex in 2001-Q1 2002; the total misstatement grew to ~$11 bn including reserve releases. CEO Bernie Ebbers (who had borrowed ~$400 m from the company to avoid selling pledged shares) got 25 years. Visible flags: (1) the line-cost/revenue (E/R) ratio held steady ~42% while the telecom industry's pricing collapsed -- 'too smooth'; (2) capex and PP&E rising while revenue growth stalled (aggressive capitalisation shows in asset-quality and depreciation ratios); (3) serial acquisitions with merger reserves that could be released into earnings; (4) huge loans to the CEO secured by pledged stock; (5) CFO vs net income gap widened when the 'capex' was stripped out. Lesson: capitalising operating costs is the simplest way to inflate EBITDA and CFO simultaneously -- check capex/sales and capex vs depreciation trends against peers; roll-ups with merger reserves are low-quality earnings.

data.early_signals: stable cost ratio in collapsing industry; rising capex/sales; serial M&A reserves; CEO loans vs pledged stock
data.lesson: Capitalised opex inflates both EBITDA and CFO; watch capex intensity

title: WorldCom (2002): capitalised line costs
